section_summary: This section records Australian and Chinese objections to Japanese fishing outside authorized waters, including the investigation and punishment of the Kosei Maru No. 2 captain. It also covers the return of Japan’s 1947–48 Antarctic whaling expedition and Australia’s opposition to a further expedition. Repeated Australian statements and U.S. drafts debate SCAP’s authority over whaling, fishing, travel, coastal patrols, and bauxite imports.

subfiles.title: Australian statement on SCAP unilateral action, continuation
subfiles.about: Australia objects to unilateral decisions on Japanese travel, fishing, and bauxite.
subfiles.summary: The statement asks for Far Eastern Commission concurrence before Japanese travel or fishing outside authorized waters and disputes the revival of Japanese aluminum production.

subfiles.title: Australian aide-mémoire on the proposed 1948–49 Antarctic whaling expedition
subfiles.about: Australia opposes a third Japanese whaling factory ship and criticizes treatment of its observer.
subfiles.summary: Australia argues that the Far Eastern Commission should decide Japanese participation, that a third ship would reduce Allied catches, and that its observer was discouraged from seeking information.

subfiles.title: Australian and Chinese Representations to Restrict Japanese Fishing Operations
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Despatch No. 234 forwards SCAP’s fishing directive and correspondence on Australian and Chinese complaints.
subfiles.summary: Sebald summarizes the Kosei Maru punishment, Chinese allegations of violations, and China’s rejection of a proposed Japanese patrol.

subfiles.title: Area Authorized for Japanese Fishing and Whaling, SCAPIN 1033
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: SCAP defines the area open to Japanese fishing and whaling.
subfiles.summary: The directive sets geographic boundaries and restrictions near certain islands, while reserving questions of sovereignty and future fishing rights.

subfiles.title: Australian report on the Kosei Maru
subfiles.about: Australia supplies identifying details for a Japanese vessel found outside permitted fishing waters.
subfiles.summary: Eckersley identifies the Kosei Maru and reports its equipment, route, and nearby vessels.

subfiles.title: SCAP reply on investigation of the Kosei Maru No. 2
subfiles.about: SCAP reports identification of the vessel and pending court proceedings.
subfiles.summary: The vessel, owner, and captain are identified; prosecution and industry disciplinary measures are pending.

subfiles.title: SCAP report on punishment of the Kosei Maru captain
subfiles.about: SCAP informs Australia of the court sentence and vessel licensing penalty.
subfiles.summary: The captain received eight months’ penal servitude and a fine; the vessel’s tuna and bonito license was to be revoked.

subfiles.title: Record of the Kosei Maru No. 2 investigation
subfiles.about: SCAP records its investigation of the vessel intercepted near Hermit Island.
subfiles.summary: The record traces the vessel’s voyage beyond the authorized fishing boundary, its interception by HMAS Australia, and interviews with Japanese fisheries officials and the captain. It notes the captain’s admitted knowledge of the boundary, planned prosecution, and efforts to prevent further violations.

subfiles.title: Chinese allegations of Japanese fishing violations
subfiles.about: China reports Japanese fishing vessels in unauthorized waters near its coast and Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: China requests investigation results and reports sightings of the Otaki Maru Nos. 31 and 32 and Kayaki Maru No. 8.

subfiles.title: SCAP reply to Chinese fishing complaints
subfiles.about: SCAP reports investigations and requests witnesses’ names for Japanese prosecutions.
subfiles.summary: SCAP says new allegations are under investigation and that appeals in earlier cases require identification of those who observed violations.

subfiles.title: Proposed Japanese patrol in the East China Sea
subfiles.about: SCAP seeks China’s view on a Japanese patrol boat to detect fishing violations.
subfiles.summary: The proposed unarmed Hatsutaka Maru would patrol a specified area and occasionally fish to help identify violators.

subfiles.title: Chinese rejection of the proposed Japanese patrol
subfiles.about: China declines to approve the Japanese East China Sea patrol proposal.
subfiles.summary: The Chinese Mission states that its government does not approve the plan.

subfiles.title: Routing note on Japanese whaling press releases
subfiles.about: A reader is asked to review and return the whaling press releases.
subfiles.summary: The note highlights three illegal whales and allocation of whale oil for Japanese consumption.

subfiles.title: Return of Japanese Antarctic Whaling Expedition
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Despatch No. 238 forwards three SCAP press releases on the expedition.
subfiles.summary: The releases cover the fleets’ return, production, and scientific whale measurements.

subfiles.title: Allied Observers with Whaling Expedition Return to Japan
subfiles.about: The Hashidate Maru returns to Osaka with Allied observers and whale products.
subfiles.summary: SCAP praises the Nippon Suisan fleet’s catch and processing efficiency, gives preliminary totals for both Japanese fleets, and describes distribution of meat and oil.

subfiles.title: Bell of Peace and Whaling Expedition Factory Ship Docks at Tokyo
subfiles.from: Far East Command Public Information Office
subfiles.about: A combined release reports a village bell gift and the Nisshin Maru’s return.
subfiles.summary: The first item describes Dr. Masuda’s planned Bell of Peace. The second reports the Taiyo Gyogyo fleet’s catch, Allied observers, regulatory violations, and whale-product distribution.

subfiles.title: Antarctic Expedition Weighs 46 Whales
subfiles.about: SCAP reports scientific measurements made during the Japanese whaling expedition.
subfiles.summary: Japanese and Allied personnel weighed blue and fin whales part by part, measured surface areas, and recorded oil yields. The release compares the results with earlier whale records and gives examples from both factory ships.

subfiles.title: MacArthur request for prompt approval of third whaling expedition
subfiles.to: Department of the Army, Undersecretary Draper; information to Department of State
subfiles.about: MacArthur seeks U.S. approval by May 1 for preparations for a third expedition.
subfiles.summary: He requests telegraphic views from interested governments to permit timely preparations, especially for a third factory ship.

subfiles.title: Australian Reaction to Matters within the Far Eastern Commission, copy
subfiles.about: Makin discusses Australian objections to SCAP actions with Saltzman.
subfiles.summary: The conversation addresses Antarctic whaling, observer treatment, Japanese travel, fishing, coastal patrols, and bauxite. Australia argues that SCAP should consult the Far Eastern Commission before acting on matters under its consideration.

subfiles.title: Australian aide-mémoire on Antarctic whaling, attached copy
subfiles.about: Australia repeats its objection to a third factory ship and reports poor treatment of its observer.
subfiles.summary: Australia seeks a Far Eastern Commission decision and argues that a third Japanese ship would reduce Allied whale-product catches.

subfiles.title: Australian statement on SCAP action, attached continuation
subfiles.about: Australia objects to unilateral decisions on Japanese travel, fishing, and bauxite.
subfiles.summary: This partial attached copy addresses proposed overseas travel, fishing near mandated territories, and revival of aluminum production.

subfiles.title: Australian Reaction to Matters within the Far Eastern Commission
subfiles.about: Makin presents Australian concerns over whaling and SCAP decisions to Saltzman.
subfiles.summary: Makin calls for Far Eastern Commission involvement in Japanese whaling, travel, fishing, coastal patrols, and bauxite imports. Saltzman stresses Japan’s food needs and says the United States will continue discussions with Australia.

subfiles.title: Australian whaling aide-mémoire, duplicate copy
subfiles.about: Australia opposes another Japanese Antarctic whaling expedition with a third factory ship.
subfiles.summary: The duplicate also complains about treatment of the Australian observer.

subfiles.title: Australian statement on unilateral SCAP decisions, duplicate copy
subfiles.about: Australia challenges SCAP action on matters it considers subject to Far Eastern Commission review.
subfiles.summary: The statement lists whaling, a SCAP press release, coastal patrols, Japanese travel and fishing, and bauxite imports. It seeks commission participation before further decisions.

subfiles.title: Australian statement on occupation policy and unilateral action
subfiles.about: Australia formally raises concerns about SCAP decisions without Far Eastern Commission approval.
subfiles.summary: This clearer copy objects to unilateral action on whaling, coastal patrols, overseas travel, fishing near Australian territories, and bauxite imports. Australia proposes taking the pattern to the commission.

subfiles.title: Draft U.S. reply to Australian objections over SCAP authority
subfiles.about: The State Department defends SCAP’s authority in response to Australia’s May 4 statement.
subfiles.summary: The draft interprets the Moscow Agreement as giving the Far Eastern Commission broad policy responsibility and SCAP executive discretion. It addresses Australian objections to a press release, coastal patrols, Japanese travel, fishing, and aluminum production. The United States argues that occupation needs, food shortages, trade, and its financial burden justify the contested actions.

subfiles.title: Clearance and routing marks for draft U.S. reply
subfiles.about: Internal clearance marks accompany the draft reply.
subfiles.summary: The page contains routing and clearance annotations, with little substantive text.

subfiles.title: Australian aide-mémoire on Antarctic whaling
subfiles.about: Australia objects to a third Japanese whaling factory ship and the treatment of its observer.
subfiles.summary: Australia seeks a Far Eastern Commission decision and cites potential harm to Allied catches.

subfiles.title: U.S. reply on the third Japanese Antarctic whaling expedition
subfiles.about: The United States explains SCAP’s decision to authorize another expedition without a third factory ship.
subfiles.summary: The reply cites Japan’s food and foreign exchange needs, maintains SCAP’s authority to approve the expedition, and promises inquiry into the Australian observer’s treatment.

subfiles.title: Policy with respect to Japanese fishing and marine industry
subfiles.about: An informal committee discusses Japanese fishing policy before Far Eastern Commission consideration.
subfiles.summary: The poorly legible memorandum records discussion of economic aspects and tactics for commission deliberation.

subfiles.title: Australian Tactics Reference FEC
subfiles.from: Hugh Borton, U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: Bullock tells Borton how Australia intends to raise its concerns.
subfiles.summary: Bullock says Evatt instructed Makin to raise whaling, bauxite, travel, and fishing in both the Department and the commission.

subfiles.title: Australian Reaction to Matters within the Far Eastern Commission, further copy
subfiles.about: Another copy records Makin’s discussion with Saltzman on whaling and SCAP authority.
subfiles.summary: Makin objects to Japanese whaling, coastal patrols, and overseas travel being authorized while the Far Eastern Commission considers them. The memorandum continues beyond page 217.
